nameStory: Cardinal flower gets its stunning name from its brilliant red flowers that match the vibrant scarlet robes worn by Catholic cardinals. The scientific name 'cardinalis' literally means 'of cardinal importance' or 'cardinal red,' cementing this plant's reputation as one of North America's most spectacular wildflowers.
description: Cardinal flower is a tall, eye-catching wildflower that produces spikes of intense scarlet-red blooms from mid to late summer. Growing 2-4 feet tall with a single, unbranched stem, this native perennial creates dramatic splashes of color along stream banks and wet meadows. The flowers are arranged in a tall cluster at the top of the plant, with lance-shaped leaves climbing up the sturdy green stem.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant scarlet-red tubular flowers with an unusual split-lip shape, arranged in a tall spike. Each flower has two upper petals and three lower ones that form a landing platform, with bright red stamens protruding from the tube.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves with serrated edges that alternate up the stem, feeling smooth but slightly firm to the touch. They're bright green and can be 2-6 inches long, getting smaller toward the top of the plant.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single, sturdy, unbranched stem rising 2-4 feet tall from the base, with the flower spike occupying the top 6-12 inches. The plant often forms small colonies from underground runners.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round seed capsules develop after flowering, splitting open to release tiny brown seeds that feel like fine dust when rubbed between fingers.

habitat: Cardinal flower thrives in consistently moist to wet soils along stream banks, pond edges, wet meadows, and swampy areas throughout New England. It prefers partial shade to full sun and is often found growing with other moisture-loving plants like monkey flower, jewelweed, and various sedges.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as a low rosette of leaves in late spring, slowly developing the central flowering stem.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through September, with the spectacular red flower spikes attracting hummingbirds and butterflies.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules mature, while leaves may turn yellowish before dying back with first frost.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground roots and runners, leaving no visible trace above ground.

funFact: Cardinal flower is like a hummingbird magnet with a built-in landing strip—its unusual flower shape evolved specifically for ruby-throated hummingbirds, and the birds' heads get dusted with pollen as they reach deep into the tubular blooms, making them the plant's primary pollinators.
confusionNotes: The brilliant red color makes cardinal flower nearly unmistakable when in bloom, though non-flowering plants might be confused with other wetland plants with similar leaves. No other New England wildflower produces flowers of this intense scarlet red.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its stunning beauty, cardinal flower contains alkaloids that make all parts of the plant toxic if ingested, so it should only be admired and never eaten. Native Americans historically used it medicinally but recognized its potent and potentially dangerous properties.
compareHints: Cardinal flower stands out dramatically from its lobelia relatives—while great blue lobelia produces similar tubular flowers in blue, and Indian tobacco has tiny pale flowers, only cardinal flower blazes in brilliant red. The flower spike shape is shared with great blue lobelia, but the colors make them unmistakable from each other.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its showier relatives cardinal flower (bright red) and great blue lobelia (deep blue), Indian tobacco has much smaller, paler flowers.
Among New England's lobelias, great blue lobelia is easily distinguished by its brilliant blue color and robust size.
Unlike its showy red cousin cardinal flower or the tall blue spikes of great blue lobelia, water lobelia is the only member of the lobelia family that lives completely underwater.
Among New England's lobelias, pale-spiked lobelia is the wallflower of the family with its subtle white or pale blue flowers.
Kalm's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its showy relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue, much larger).
Garden lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its New England native relatives like cardinal flower and great blue lobelia, which are tall, upright wetland plants.

Unlike its native Lobelia relatives such as cardinal flower or great blue lobelia which grow as upright leafy stems with showy flower spikes, matted pratia is a tiny mat-forming groundcover with individual star-shaped flowers.
Nuttall's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its famous relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue and tall).
